lessons.title: What is Cash Flow and a Budget?
lessons.learningGoal: By the end of this lesson, you'll understand what a budget is, why it's important, and how to calculate basic cash flow.

microLessonContent.text: Meet Abigail! Abigail is a single mom with twin 14-year-olds.
She manages all her family's expenses, including paying for her children's activities.
For fun, Abigail likes to go rock climbing and swim at her apartment complex's pool.
Juggling everything going on in her life, Abigail feels like she isn't in control of her money.
She wishes that she had a clearer view of her spending so she could cut unnecessary spending and save up for a future vacation.
To help her feel in control of her money, Abigail has decided to create a budget.
A budget is simply a plan for your money. It's a tool you can use to help make financial decisions.
Budgets involve two main categories: income and expenses.

knowledgeChecks.question: What is the purpose of a budget?

answerChoices.text: To help you feel in control of your money

knowledgeChecks.explanation: The purpose of a budget helps you feel in control of your money by laying out all your income and expenses and creating a plan for your money.

knowledgeChecks.question: True or False? You should create a budget to help you track where your money is going.
knowledgeChecks.explanation: Creating a budget does help you track where your money is going.

knowledgeChecks.question: When creating a budget, what are the two main categories that you need to track?

answerChoices.text: Credit card debt and unused balance of credit card
Retirement accounts and interest from a CD that will mature 5 years from now.

knowledgeChecks.explanation: Budgeting manages the money that you earn (income) with the expenses that you have.

microLessonContent.text: Meet Ramona! She is an 18-year-old college Freshman.
Ramona has a part-time federal work-study job at her campus dining hall.

Ramona receives federal student loans to cover her tuition, room, and board.
The money she earns from her job goes towards groceries, textbooks, fun concerts, and her bowling league.
Cash flow is tracking the money you earn and the money you're spending.
Money In (Income) - Money Out (Expenses) = Cash Flow

As a Registered Nurse (RN), Abigail earns $7,500 per month. Her total monthly expenses are $2,154.

$7,500 (Income) - $2,154 (Expenses) = $5,346 (Net Cash Flow)
So Abigail's total cash flow each month is about $5,346.

knowledgeChecks.question: How do you calculate cash flow?
knowledgeChecks.explanation: Cash flow describes the movement of cash moving into and out of an account over a specific period. Income - Expenses = Cash Flow.

knowledgeChecks.question: Ramona earns $1,200 per month and spends $1,000 per month. How much does Beaver have at the end of each month?
knowledgeChecks.explanation: Ramona's Cash Flow monitors how much cash is moving into and out of Ramona's account. Within the same month, Ramona's Income( $1,200) - Ramona's Expenses ( $1500) = Ramona's Cash Flow ( $500). Ramona has more incoming money than outgoing money so Ramona has positive Cash Flow.

knowledgeChecks.question: What are the two numbers you need to calculate cash flow (select all that apply)?
knowledgeChecks.explanation: Cash Flow considers incoming cash from all sources of income and all cash that is outgoing to pay for expenses within a period of time.

lessons.title: Income
lessons.learningGoal: By the end of this lesson, you'll be able to identify different sources of income, calculate monthly income, and explain the difference between gross pay and net pay.

microLessonContent.text: There are many different sources of income.Some common sources of income include:

items: Alimony from a divorce or separation
Government Benefits like Social Security or Unemployment Benefits

microLessonContent.text: Abigail, our single mom of two, makes income as a Registered nurse and receives child support from her ex-husband. So, her two sources of income are her paychecks and monthly child support.
Ramona, on the other hand, only has income from her part-time campus position. So her sole source of income is from her paychecks.

knowledgeChecks.question: What is an example of income?
knowledgeChecks.explanation: Paychecks, child support, interest earned on investments, and sales of goods are just some examples of sources of income.

knowledgeChecks.question: True or False? Income only includes the money you make from a job.
knowledgeChecks.explanation: There are multiple types of income. Paychecks, child support, interest earned on investments, and sales of goods are just some examples of sources of income.

knowledgeChecks.question: Select Abigail's source(s) of income (select all that apply)
knowledgeChecks.explanation: Abigail's sources of income include both her paycheck and child support payments.

microLessonContent.text: Abigail receives a bi-weekly paycheck from her job and a monthly child support check.
Paychecks are commonly paid on a weekly, bi-weekly, or semi-monthly schedule.
Abigail is paid bi-weekly, which means she receives a paycheck every two weeks for a total of 26 paychecks per year.
If Abigail were paid semi-monthly, she would receive 24 paychecks per year on the same two dates each month.
Common semi-monthly pay dates are the 1st and 15th or the 15th and last day of the month.

knowledgeChecks.question: Select the most common pay frequencies for paychecks (select all that apply):
knowledgeChecks.explanation: Paychecks are usually paid weekly, bi-weekly, and semi-monthly. The decision is made by the employer.

knowledgeChecks.question: How many paychecks does Abigail receive per year since she is paid on a bi-weekly basis?
knowledgeChecks.explanation: Bi-weekly paychecks will total 26 paychecks per year. Semi-monthly paychecks will count towards 24 paychecks per year.

knowledgeChecks.question: True or false? Semi-monthly paychecks are paid on the same 2 dates every month?
knowledgeChecks.explanation: Usually, semi-monthly paychecks are paid to employees consistently on the same 2 dates every month.

knowledgeChecks.question:
Let's help Abigail calculate her income.

Abigail works a full-time job as a nurse at the local hospital. She makes $84,000 a year after taxes are taken out. What is her monthly income? (Hint: Divide total yearly income by 12 to get monthly income)
knowledgeChecks.explanation: Divide the total yearly income by 12. Abigail earns $84,000/12 = $7,000 per month

microLessonContent.text: When Abigail looks at her latest paystub, she sees that she made a total of $3,500 for the past 2 weeks. However, she only receives $2,700 in her bank account. Why is that?
The total amount that Abigail sees on her paycheck of $3,500 is called her gross pay.
Gross pay is the total amount of money earned in that pay period before any deductions. The $3,500 is her gross pay.
So then why did she receive $800 less in her bank account?

The $2,700 she received in her bank account is called her Net pay or 'take home pay'.Net pay is your gross total pay minus payroll deductions like taxes and any employer benefits that you pay into like health insurance or retirement plans.
Gross Pay - Taxes/Benefits = Net Pay (Take Home Pay)

knowledgeChecks.question: Gross Pay is:

answerChoices.text: The amount you take home after deductions
The total amount earned before deductions
The amount deposited into your bank account

knowledgeChecks.explanation: Gross pay is your total pay before you take out taxes and any employer benefits you might be paying into.

knowledgeChecks.question: Net pay is:

answerChoices.text: The total amount earned before deductions

knowledgeChecks.explanation: Net pay is your “take home pay”. It's your total pay (gross pay) minus the payroll deductions.

knowledgeChecks.question: If Ramona works 20 hours per week for $15 per hour, what is Ramona's gross pay for one week?
What is the correct formula for calculating your net pay?

answerChoices.text: Payroll deductions - Gross Pay = Net Pay
Gross Pay - Payroll deductions = Net Pay
Gross Pay + Payroll Deductions = Net Pay
Payroll Deductions x Gross Pay = Net Pay

knowledgeChecks.explanation: Gross Pay - Payroll deductions = Net Pay. Net pay is your “take home pay”. It's your total pay (gross pay) minus the payroll deductions.

lessons.title: Understanding Needs vs Wants
lessons.learningGoal: By the end of this lesson, you'll be able to identify the difference between needs and wants, as well as categorizing common expenses into each group.

microLessonContent.text: Learning the difference between a need and a want empowers you to create a budget.
Needs are essential expenses for survival or well-being such as medical care, transportation, food, and shelter.
Wants are anything non-essential that enhances your life.
Needs and wants depend on your personal situation - what is a 'want' for one person might be a 'need' for another person.

knowledgeChecks.question: What would be an example of a need?
knowledgeChecks.explanation: As fun as plushies, going to the movies and concerts are, you will survive without these things. However, without food, you would not be able to survive.

knowledgeChecks.question: What would be an example of a want?
knowledgeChecks.explanation: Food, shelter, and transportation to work are all important for survival and are basic needs. A new boardgame is fun, but you will survive without it.

knowledgeChecks.question: True or false? Needs and wants are the same for everyone.
knowledgeChecks.explanation: Needs and wants are different for each person. Something one person considers a need may be a want for someone else. For example, a car may be a need for someone who commutes to work, but a want for someone who has reliable public transportation.

knowledgeChecks.question: Which of Abigail's expenses is a want?
knowledgeChecks.explanation: For Abigail, rock climbing is a recreational activity, making it a want rather than an essential expense needed for daily living.
